source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11) Conceptual blending: network types
finding: Gives the four network types. Simplex: one input holds an organising frame, the other holds specific values, and values fill the frame roles. Mirror: one shared organising frame in all spaces. Single-scope: two different frames, only one projected into the blend. Double-scope: two different frames, parts of both go into the blend.
numbers: Four types; no counts or effect sizes given.
limits: Secondary source. It gives no example for three of the four types. It reports no empirical test of the typology itself.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean choice rule for a blend operator: same frame (mirror), frame plus values (simplex), one frame wins (single-scope), both frames contribute (double-scope).
quote: A mirror network is characterised by a shared organising frame present in each of the mental spaces.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11) Conceptual blending: criticism section (reports Gibbs 2000; Ritchie 2004)
finding: Main critics say blending theory has no testable hypotheses, so it cannot predict behaviour. Gibbs (2000) calls it a framework, not a single theory, and says other theories explain the same data. Ritchie (2004) says many blends can be explained by simpler integration, and the monk riddle has another reading.
numbers: No numbers. Fauconnier is said to have answered the critics (cited 2020/2021).
limits: Secondhand summary of the original papers, which were not opened (publisher page returned HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: The typology is descriptive. Treat it as a design heuristic, not as a validated causal model.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11) Conceptual blending: empirical tests
finding: The page cites no direct empirical test of the four network types. It cites only cognitive-modelling and computational-creativity work (Lieto et al.) for the wider blending framework.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence on a short page, not proof that none exists. Keyword searches of arXiv and Europe PMC (see b28) also found none.
agent_relevance: Do not claim the double-scope-for-novelty rule is proven. It is a hypothesis for our agent to test.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study (Memory & Cognition)
finding: ERPs from 18 adults reading sentences ending in literal, metaphoric, or 'literal mapping' words (literal sense, but prompts mapping from another domain). N400 at 300-500 ms was smallest for literal, largest for metaphor, intermediate for literal mapping. Metaphors also gave a larger posterior positivity.
numbers: N = 18; three conditions; graded N400: literal < literal mapping < metaphor.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC); full PDF was not reachable. It supports 'integration cost grows with mapping demand', not any particular network type. Authors call it consistent with blending, not proof.
agent_relevance: Best human evidence that distant-domain integration costs more effort. A double-scope blend should be expected to cost more steps and to need a check stage.
quote: Literal endings elicited the smallest N400, metaphors the largest N400, whereas literal mappings elicited an N400 of intermediate amplitude.

source: Jonczyk et al. (2020) Engineering creativity: prior experience modulates electrophysiological responses to novel metaphors (Psychophysiology)
finding: A blending-inspired ERP design replicated the graded N400: anomalous > novel metaphor > literal. Engineers had a smaller N400 for engineering novel metaphors than non-engineers, so prior domain knowledge cuts integration cost.
numbers: Engineering vs non-engineering students; N400 maximal to anomalous, then metaphorical, then literal. The knowledge effect came from planned comparisons; the sentence type x knowledge x group interaction was NOT significant.
limits: Sample sizes not extracted. The knowledge effect rests on planned comparisons without the full interaction, so it is weaker than it sounds.
agent_relevance: Moderator: expertise lowers blend cost. A blend between two frames the model knows well needs less checking than one with a thin frame; give the model frame facts first.
quote: a mirror effect on the N400 to novel metaphorical sentences, with attenuated N400 in engineers and enhanced N400 in non-engineers

source: Miller, Jonczyk, Zaharchuk & van Hell (2025) Unlocking second language novel metaphor processing (Psychophysiology)
finding: Same design as the 2020 monolingual study, run on second-language English users. An N400 anomaly effect appeared at the sentence end, with no significant difference between metaphorical and literal. L2 users made more sentence-evaluation errors, especially on anomalous sentences, so conceptual expansion looked more effortful in L2.
numbers: Single-trial ERP plus behaviour; L2 users vs an earlier monolingual study.
limits: Compared against a previous study, not a concurrent control group. Blending is one of several accounts (career of metaphor, relevance theory) that predict the same pattern.
agent_relevance: Rival theories predict the same graded N400, so ERP data cannot pick blending over analogy. A discriminating test would manipulate which frame structure is projected.

source: Miller et al. (2025), literature review section (cites Arzouan 2007; Lai 2009; Rutter 2012; De Grauwe 2010)
finding: Several ERP studies find the same ordering (literal < novel metaphor < anomalous) and read it as blending-style mapping effort. The review lists three accounts that explain it equally: structure mapping/comparison, career of metaphor, relevance theory.
numbers: Cited studies: Coulson & Van Petten 2002, 2007; Arzouan 2007; Lai 2009; De Grauwe 2010; Rataj 2017; Schneider 2014; Jankowiak 2017.
limits: Citations seen only inside the 2025 paper; the originals were not opened.
agent_relevance: Blending has indirect, non-discriminating support. The N400 pattern is a cost signal, not a test of the four types.

source: Canovas & Manzanares (2014) Conceptual mappings and neural reuse (Front Hum Neurosci)
finding: Short commentary placing blending theory beside conceptual metaphor theory and neural reuse, and pointing to material anchors for blends (mental timeline, SNARC effect) as the testable part. No network-type experiment.
numbers: About 20,000 characters, no experiments. 22 mentions of blending; 0 mentions of single-scope, double-scope, simplex or mirror network.
limits: Commentary, not a test. Shows that even a blending-friendly neuroscience paper does not use the four-type typology.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the typology is rarely operationalised outside Fauconnier and Turner's own work.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual integration networks, Cognitive Science 22(2)
finding: Founding source of the four network types and the optimality principles (integration, topology, pattern completion, unpacking, web, relevance). Not read: the web copy returned only front matter (91 pages, 24,295 words).
numbers: No numbers: a theory paper built on worked examples.
limits: opened:false. No body text retrieved. Type definitions in b01 come from Wikipedia, not this paper.
agent_relevance: Source to read next for exact definitions and the optimality principles, which Ge & Parikh (2021) already used as evaluation questions.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (2002) The way we think; Turner (2014) The origin of ideas
finding: Books that claim double-scope blending is the engine of human creativity. Cited from general knowledge only.
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: opened:false. The claim is theoretical. No study found that sorts real creative products by network type and measures novelty.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'double-scope for novel ideas' premise in our schema row. Unverified.

source: Ge & Parikh (2021) Visual Conceptual Blending with Large-scale Language and Vision Models
finding: A language model proposes the blend description, a CLIP-guided image model draws it. Language models beat the ConceptNet knowledge base at finding properties on the simile dataset. Human questions came from the optimality principles. CLIP-based BigSleep and DeepDaze beat DF-GAN.
numbers: Table 3 precision (P@10 / P@100 / P@1000), rows partly garbled in the PDF: BERT-base 1.12 / 2.70 / 5.90; BERT-large 0.13 / 7.69 / 37.33; GPT row 1.59 / 15.72 / 53.08; best row 2.59 / 24.84 / 66.38. 20 blend descriptions; 6 questions; each comparison answered by 9 AMT subjects.
limits: Model names beyond BERT and GPT uncertain because pdftotext garbled the table. Image quality limited by the generator. No network type is varied.
agent_relevance: LLM-style models can supply the property links a blend needs, and the optimality principles can be turned into scoring questions. Pairwise-judge format is reusable.

source: Ge & Parikh (2021), human evaluation design
finding: The six human questions map to Fauconnier and Turner's optimality principles: questions 1 and 2 test unpacking (can you recognise each input), 3 and 4 test integration (does it blend and fit the description), 5 and 6 test general quality.
numbers: 6 questions x 3 model pairs x 20 descriptions x 9 subjects each.
limits: Principles, not network types, were operationalised.
agent_relevance: A blend-check stage can ask: can each input still be recognised, does the blend fit the stated target, is it interesting.

source: Chakrabarty, Muresan & Peng (2020) simile dataset, as used by Ge & Parikh (2021)
finding: The simile dataset (literal sentence paired with its simile form) was the test bed for the reasoning phase: given Source and Target, can the model rank the right shared property.
numbers: Pairs of <Source, Target>; example <The city was beautiful, ...>.
limits: A simile is mostly a single-scope or mirror-like mapping, not a double-scope blend.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks used so far for LLM blending cover the easy end of the typology.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Probing and Inducing Combinational Creativity in Vision-Language Models
finding: Builds on Fauconnier and Turner and tests 11 models on a 666-mashup dataset (CreativeMashup) with three levels: identification, explanation, implication. Top models beat average people but not experts.
numbers: Implication winning rate: human experts 78.3, GPT-4o 73.5, GPT-4V 71.9, Gemini-1.5-Pro 71.7, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 62.9, average people 51.0, Claude-3-Opus 39.2, LLaVA-1.6-34B 40.6, LLaVA-1.5-7B 20.1. Identification precision/recall: GPT-4o 75.67/85.00; people 53.42/70.33. Explanation precision: GPT-4o 74.19, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 74.19, people 69.89.
limits: Judged by GPT-4o against two human experts (agreement 85.1% and 81.6% on 200 comparisons), so self-preference is possible. Mashups are two physical objects, not abstract frames.
agent_relevance: Models understand blends better than average people; the implication step is the weakest. A blend operator should spend its checking effort on implications.

source: Peng et al. (2025), fusion vs replacement comparison
finding: The dataset has two combination types: fusion (traits of both objects merged) and replacement (one object takes the other's place). The text says 9 of 11 models had higher identification precision for fusion. This is a rough analogue of double-scope-like vs single-scope-like blends.
numbers: 9 of 11 models. The Figure 5 caption says the reverse (replacement higher than fusion), so the paper contradicts itself.
limits: Self-contradiction: text says fusion higher, caption says replacement higher. The two types are not Fauconnier and Turner's types. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Combination type changes how hard a blend is to decode. Do not rely on the direction until the figure is checked.

source: Peng et al. (2025), Identification-Explanation-Implication (IEI) prompting for generation
finding: A three-step scaffold (name the inputs, explain how they combine, state the implication) before image generation improved creative quality over a plain two-object prompt (II). The gain was not caused by longer prompts.
numbers: Midjourney winning rate 0.26 to 0.35 under IEI. Prompt length II mean 487.95 vs IEI 514.53, t = -0.84, p = 0.404. In 46.0% of IEI wins the IEI prompt was shorter. GPT-4o concept integration succeeded in 36 of 40 (90%) DALLE-3 cases; 10 of 36 (27.8%) good descriptions still failed in the image model.
limits: Gain is larger for stronger models; Stable Diffusion 3 showed minimal gain. Image generation is the bottleneck, so text-only agents may see a different size of effect.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a scaffold step: explain how the two frames combine before producing the blend, then state implications.

source: Olearo et al. (2025) Blending Concepts with Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
finding: Four zero-shot blending methods in a diffusion model (textual embedding mix, U-Net, alternate, switch). No single method wins in every scenario. Prompt order matters.
numbers: 100 participants, 22 concept pairs. Alternate over Switch 51% (p=0.31, not significant); Alternate over Textual 60%; Alternate over U-Net 57%; Switch over Textual 61%; Switch over U-Net 58%; U-Net over Textual 55% (all p<0.001).
limits: Image models, not language. Single-word prompts. General-public sample, no expert raters.
agent_relevance: Order of the two inputs can flip a blend. Try both directions, or record which input supplies the frame (single-scope).

source: Olearo et al. (2025), limitations section
finding: Authors state the user study does not test seed variability, uses short single-word prompts, and a general-public sample. They suggest studies with art, design or psychology experts.
numbers: 100 participants; 22 pairs.
limits: No test across network types.
agent_relevance: Gap: no one has varied network type and measured outcome.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: Conceptual Blending, Neural Dynamics, and Prompt-Induced Transitions in LLMs
finding: A review-style paper mapping input spaces to prompt concepts, the generic space to pretraining knowledge, and the blend to model output. It defines Prompt-Induced Transition (tone or meaning shift) and Prompt-Induced Hallucination (blending distant domains, e.g. periodic table with tarot).
numbers: No measured results. It claims repeated elicitation across models with no counts, and proposes entropy and head-ablation studies as future work.
limits: Speculative. No data, no baselines, no network-type analysis. Not usable as evidence of effect.
agent_relevance: Warning, not evidence: blending distant domains can give fluent but ungrounded output. A double-scope blend needs a grounding check before it is kept.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Misty: UI Prototyping Through Interactive Conceptual Blending (CHI 2025)
finding: An LLM tool that blends a source UI with example UIs. 14 frontend developers did blending tasks. Users liked broad control, but outputs were often imperfect.
numbers: 14 participants; 103 blending operations; mean satisfaction 3.2 of 5 (median 3, SD 1.3); 44 operations rated above 3, 28 rated 3, 31 below 3. Operation use: global blending 36/103 (34.95%), drag-and-drop 35/103 (33.98%), regenerate 19/103 (18.5%), semantic diff 9/103 (8.74%), code edit 4/103 (3.88%).
limits: Small N, no control condition. Blending here means mixing two UI artefacts, not the four network types.
agent_relevance: About 30% of blend outputs disappointed even in a good tool. Plan for a reject-and-retry loop and steerable blending strength.

source: Cho et al. (2025) Imagine for Me: blended attention (IT-Blender)
finding: A method that blends a real reference image with text. The paper shows examples at the top 10%, 50% and 90% of a blending score; the weakest samples keep only one input.
numbers: Top 10/50/90 percentile samples shown for SD1.5 and FLUX; no headline number extracted.
limits: Only qualitative figures and appendix text were read.
agent_relevance: Failure shape worth copying into a checker: the blend keeps only one input (collapses to single-scope by accident).

source: Matsuhira et al. (2024) Investigating conceptual blending of a diffusion model for nonword-to-image generation
finding: Stable Diffusion text embeddings were interpolated between two concepts. Blended Concept Depiction (BCD) and Mixed Concept Depiction (MCD) were highest at the midpoint ratio 0.5.
numbers: At ratio 0.5: BCD 0.621, MCD 0.862. Over all ratios: BCD 0.389, MCD 0.471. 1,000 supports in total; ground-truth embeddings gave BCD in up to 60% of images.
limits: Narrow blend definition and automated classifier judges. Not a language task.
agent_relevance: Equal weighting of two inputs gave the most real blends. Heavy weighting of one input gave single-scope-like collapse.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Beyond Pixels: Visual Metaphor Transfer via Schema-Driven Agentic Reasoning
finding: A multi-agent framework built on Conceptual Blending Theory with schema extraction, a transfer agent, and a diagnostic agent with backtracking. It beat four baselines (GPT-Image, Banana-pro, Midjourney, BAGEL) in judged metaphor quality and a 100-person human study.
numbers: Human study N = 100 (45 male, 55 female). Task 1 means: Metaphor Ingenuity 4.61, Violation Appropriateness 4.49, Visual Integration 4.77, Visual Quality 4.79. Task 2 'Ours better': 64.44% vs GPT-Image, 67.11% vs Banana-pro, 72.89% vs Midjourney, 76.22% vs BAGEL; judged worse in under 10% of pairs. Aesthetic score 5.68; 16.8% rise on the AA metric over runner-up.
limits: Ablations (no transfer agent, no diagnostic, no backtracking, no CBT description, one-shot CBT prompt) are shown but their numbers were not extracted. Baselines get a plain prompt, so gains mix scaffold with extra steps.
agent_relevance: Closest existing system to our scaffold idea: extract each frame's schema, transfer, diagnose, backtrack. Staged blending with a diagnosis step beat one-shot prompting.

source: Meanings are like Onions (2025) layered approach to metaphor processing
finding: Position paper proposing three layers for metaphor handling: content analysis, conceptual blending analysis, pragmatic intent. Notes that no dataset annotates attitude or speech act, and that blend-structure annotation is thin.
numbers: No experiments. Describes a Blending Ontology that encodes four-space networks and a weapon-frame example (cigarette as bullet).
limits: No measured results. The ontology encodes the four spaces, not the four network types.
agent_relevance: As of mid-2025 no gold-standard data labels blends by network type. Our evaluation must build its own.

source: Pop-Blends (Wang et al. 2023 version) PopBlends: Strategies for Conceptual Blending with Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 plus a knowledge base suggests pop-culture blends. In a within-subject study people made about twice as many blend ideas as with a search baseline, with less mental demand.
numbers: 10 participants. Ideas per pair 2.03 (SD 0.84) vs 0.87 (SD 0.56), Wilcoxon p<0.001. NASA-TLX mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004); effort p=0.006. Top-1 connecting-concept accuracy 56.0%, 55.3%, 58.7% across three GPT strategies; at least one of five correct 90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3%. GPT-3 attribute accuracy 57% overall (adjectives 79%, activities 58%, catchphrases 35%).
limits: Small N (10 students). GPT-3 invented attributes; catchphrases were wrong 65% of the time. Blends are mostly mirror-like (shared connecting concept), not double-scope.
agent_relevance: Two stages help: pick a connecting concept, then generate scenes. Take five candidates and keep any good one, since top-1 is only about 56% right. Verify generated attributes.

source: PopBlends, scene-stage relatedness
finding: Second-stage scenes were more often related to the connecting concept for product scenes than for pop-culture scenes. GPT-3 sometimes pretends to make connections.
numbers: Product scenes related 89.1% vs 75.9% for pop-culture scenes (adjusted); raw 80.0% vs 63.4%. Annotator agreement (IRR) for attributes 0.32 to 0.47.
limits: Low annotator agreement. 10 annotators.
agent_relevance: Scene quality depends on how well known the domain is, again pointing to the expertise moderator. Check grounding for the thin-frame input.

source: Lieto et al. (2019/2020), PET-FISH concept combination framework, as cited on Wikipedia
finding: Wikipedia cites Lieto and colleagues as having tested a concept-combination (PET-FISH) framework with blending in cognitive modelling. Original not opened.
numbers: None obtained.
limits: opened:false.
agent_relevance: A place to look for modelled tests of how two concepts combine.

source: Search gap check: arXiv and Europe PMC keyword searches for network-type terms
finding: A search of arXiv for the exact phrase double-scope returned no papers. A Europe PMC search for double-scope returned mostly endoscopy papers. A Europe PMC blending-theory plus ERP search returned N400 metaphor studies, none about network types.
numbers: arXiv 'double-scope': 0 results. arXiv 'conceptual blending' plus language model: 5 results. arXiv 'conceptual blending theory': 23 results, about 4 using AI systems. Europe PMC double-scope: 161 hits, nearly all medical.
limits: Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API returned 429 rate limits, so only keyword search pages worked. Papers using other words (bisociation, concept combination) would be missed.
agent_relevance: Strong signal that no study has varied network type and measured the effect on human or LLM output. Treat 'double-scope for novelty' as untested and plan our own A/B test.

source: Arithmetic of formal blending: Artificial Mathematical Intelligence paper (arXiv 2112.02457)
finding: Formal route: blending done in the Heterogeneous Tool Set (HETS) over CASL specifications produced the notion of a topological group from continuous functions and groups, in three different specifications.
numbers: Three specifications; one concept; three authors.
limits: Abstract page only. One worked example, no benchmark, no network-type labels.
agent_relevance: Shows blending can be run as a formal operation with a checker, but only where domains have formal structure.
